claim: A significant portion of human cancers utilize a recombination-based pathway, alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), to maintain telomere length.
source: A significant portion of human cancers utilize a recombination-based pathway, alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), to maintain telomere length.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cancer biology supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: The terminal portions of chromosomes in ALT cells contain canonical telomeric sequences with the same terminus bias (-ATC) observed in non-ALT cells.
source: Our data reveal that the terminal portions of chromosomes in ALT cells contain canonical telomeric sequences with the same terminus bias (-ATC) observed in non-ALT cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by END-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript showing terminal sequence analysis.

claim: POT1 is required to preserve the precise regulation of the 5′ end in cells that maintain telomere length using the ALT pathway.
source: Furthermore, as reported for non-ALT cells, POT1 is required to preserve the precise regulation of the 5′ end in cells that maintain telomere length using the ALT pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing POT1 depletion effects in ALT cells.

claim: The regulation of the terminal 5′ of chromosomes occurs independently of the mechanism of telomere elongation.
source: Thus, the regulation of the terminal 5′ of chromosomes occurs independently of the mechanism of telomere elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ALT and non-ALT cells showing similar terminal sequences.

claim: Human telomeres consist of 5–15 kilobases of repetitive DNA sequences (5′-TTAGGG-3′).
source: Human telomeres consist of 5–15 kilobases of repetitive DNA sequences (5′-TTAGGG-3′), which serve as a binding platform for an essential protective protein complex named shelterin (Palm and de Lange, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in telomere biology, supported by citation to Palm and de Lange, 2008.

claim: The terminal portion of chromosomes is composed of a single-stranded 3′ overhang of approximately 200 nucleotides.
source: The terminal portion of chromosomes is composed of a single-stranded 3′ overhang of approximately 200 nucleotides, generated by the interplay between DNA replication and end-processing, and regulated by the telomere-associated protein POT1 (Cai and de Lange, 2023; Lim and Cech, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent reviews on telomere structure.

claim: At leading strand telomeres, the newly synthesized DNA terminates in a blunt end and requires post-replicative resection by nucleases such as Apollo and Exo1.
source: At leading strand telomeres, the newly synthesized DNA terminates in a blunt end and requires post-replicative resection by nucleases such as Apollo and Exo1 and a fill-in action promoted by CST complex to create the 5′ overhang (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2012 describing telomere end processing mechanisms.

claim: Lagging strand synthesis inherently generates a 3′ overhang due to Okazaki fragment processing.
source: In contrast, lagging strand synthesis inherently generates a 3′ overhang due to Okazaki fragment processing, where removal of the terminal RNA primer leaves a single-stranded gap that is partially filled in by DNA polymerase α-primase with the aid of the CST complex (Takai et al., 2024; for reviews, see Cai and de Lange, 2023; Lim and Cech, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing DNA replication mechanisms at telomeres.

claim: Progressive loss of telomeric repeats during DNA replication leads to telomere shortening and represents a barrier to unlimited proliferation.
source: Progressive loss of telomeric repeats during DNA replication leads to telomere shortening and represents a barrier to unlimited proliferation (Feldser and Greider, 2007; Greenberg et al., 1998; Greider, 1996; Perera et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations on telomere biology.

claim: Approximately 85% of cancers activate telomerase to synthesize new telomeric repeats.
source: To overcome this tumor suppressive barrier, ~85% of cancers activate telomerase, a reverse transcriptase, to synthesize new telomeric repeats (Shay and Bacchetti, 1997; Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a well-established statistic in cancer biology supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 15% of cancers engage the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway.
source: The remaining ~15% of cancers engage the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) pathway, a recombination-based mechanism to elongate telomeres using existing telomeric DNA as a template (Dunham et al., 2000; Bryan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a well-established statistic in cancer biology supported by citations.

claim: Virtually all (99.9%) telomeric END-seq reads correspond to the C-rich strand in HeLa and RPE1 cells.
source: Strikingly, virtually all (99.9%) telomeric END-seq reads correspond to the C-rich strand, in agreement with the fact that chromosome ends are one-ended DSBs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The vast majority (78% and 65% for HeLa and RPE1, respectively) of chromosomes end with ATC-5′.
source: This analysis shows that the vast majority (78% and 65% for HeLa and RPE1, respectively) of chromosomes end with ATC-5′ (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data presented in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The ATC-5′ terminal sequence is in agreement with previous data obtained using STELA on defined chromosome ends in HeLa cells.
source: Strikingly, this is in agreement with previous data obtained using a PCR-based approach termed STELA on defined chromosome ends in HeLa cells (Sfeir et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim compares current findings with previously published data.

claim: Chromosome ends show a strong bias for ATC-5′ as a terminal sequence in human, mouse, and dog cell lines.
source: In these experiments, we found that chromosome ends show a strong bias for ATC-5′ as a terminal sequencing (Figure 1D), in line with previous findings (Tesmer et al., 2023; Smoom et al., 2023), suggesting a conserved mechanism for its generation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data across multiple species and citations to previous work.

claim: T7 exonuclease treatment prior to END-seq is sufficient to change the bias of the ATC-5′ sequence.
source: As shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, T7-treated samples display an altered distribution of telomeric permutations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing changes in sequence distribution after T7 treatment.

claim: POT1-depleted cells have a significant reduction in terminal repeats ending with the canonical ATC-5′ sequence.
source: In agreement with previously published data, END-seq analysis showed that POT1-depleted cells have a significant reduction in terminal repeats ending with the canonical ATC-5′ sequence (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by END-seq data from POT1 depletion experiments.

claim: Depletion of POT1a altered 5′ termini in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: END-seq analysis revealed that while depletion of POT1a altered 5′ termini, depletion of POT1b had no effect (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Depletion of POT1b had no effect on 5′ termini in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: END-seq analysis revealed that while depletion of POT1a altered 5′ termini, depletion of POT1b had no effect (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: POT1a plays a dominant role in maintaining proper 5′ end processing compared to POT1b.
source: This striking result highlights a fundamental difference between POT1a and POT1b, demonstrating that POT1a plays a dominant role in maintaining proper 5′ end processing, consistent with recently published work (Tesmer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to recent work.

claim: In ALT cells, the vast majority of telomeric reads (82–98% across 3 cell lines and 11 biological repeats) correspond to the C-rich strand.
source: Our analysis shows that in ALT cells, the vast majority of telomeric reads (82–98% across 3 cell lines and 11 biological repeats) correspond to the C-rich strand (Figure 3A–C), consistent with non-ALT cells and the expected pattern for a one-ended-DSB.
evidence: This is supported by END-seq data from multiple ALT cell lines shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: The majority of telomeric reads in all three tested ALT cell lines start with the canonical ATC-5′ sequence.
source: Motif analysis revealed that the majority of telomeric reads in all three tested cell lines start with the canonical ATC-5′ sequence (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data from ALT cell lines.

claim: POT1 depletion in U2OS cells resulted in formation of 53BP1 foci.
source: POT1 depletion resulted in formation of 53BP1 foci (Figure 3E and F), consistent with POT1's established role in suppressing the DNA damage response at chromosome ends (Hockemeyer et al., 2005; Denchi and de Lange, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and citations to previous work on POT1 function.

claim: Depletion of POT1 dramatically altered the 5′ natural termini in ALT-positive cell lines.
source: The data show that, similarly to telomerase-positive HeLa cells, depletion of POT1 dramatically altered the 5′ natural termini in ALT-positive cell lines (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by END-seq data from POT1-depleted ALT cells.

claim: VTRs in ALT-positive cells do not occur more frequently than non-ALT cells within the very terminal portion of chromosome ends.
source: This result shows that in ALT-positive cells, VTRs do not occur more frequently than non-ALT cells within the very terminal portion of chromosome ends.
evidence: This is based on analysis of variant telomeric repeats in the first 30 nucleotides from the 5′ end.

claim: S1-END-seq in ALT-negative cells revealed only C-strand telomeric reads excluding the presence of a significant amount of ssDNA within the telomeric tract.
source: S1-END-seq in ALT-negative cells revealed only C-strand telomeric reads excluding the presence of a significant amount of ssDNA within the telomeric tract in these cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by S1-END-seq experimental data from ALT-negative cells.

claim: S1-END-seq on ALT-positive cell lines revealed that G-rich and C-rich telomeric reads were detected at similar frequencies.
source: By contrast, performing S1-END-seq on a panel of ALT-positive cell lines revealed that G-rich and C-rich telomeric reads were detected at similar frequencies (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by S1-END-seq experimental data from ALT-positive cells.

claim: Telomeres in ALT-positive cells contain frequent regions of single-stranded DNA.
source: These data show that telomeres in ALT-positive cells contain frequent regions of single-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the S1-END-seq data showing similar G-rich and C-rich reads in ALT cells.

claim: The ratio of C-rich to G-rich reads in S1-END-seq data can distinguish ALT-negative (0.98–0.99) from ALT-positive cell lines (0.4–0.58).
source: Furthermore, our data shows that the ratio of C-rich to G-rich reads in S1-END-seq data can distinguish ALT-negative (0.98–0.99) from ALT-positive cell lines (0.4–0.58).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of S1-END-seq data from multiple cell lines.

claim: ALT-positive cells analyzed contain a minimum of three single-stranded telomeric DNA regions per chromosome end.
source: Based on this ratio, we estimate that the ALT-positive cells analyzed here contain a minimum of three single-stranded telomeric DNA regions per chromosome end (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is estimated from the C/G strand ratio in S1-END-seq data.

claim: BLM-deficient U2OS cells show a bias toward C-rich reads (C/G strand ratio: 0.7) in S1-END-seq.
source: By contrast, BLM-deficient U2OS cells show a bias toward C-rich reads (C/G strand ratio: 0.7, Figure 4D), indicating that these cells have reduced levels of ssDNA at chromosome ends compared to the parental ALT-positive U2OS cell line (at least one ssDNA region per chromosome end).
evidence: This is supported by S1-END-seq data from BLM-deficient cells.

claim: Expression of TRF1-FokI nuclease in BLM-deficient cells was sufficient to induce single-stranded telomeric DNA at telomeres.
source: Expression of the TRF1-FokI nuclease in BLM-deficient cells was sufficient to induce single-stranded telomeric DNA at telomeres as seen by ssTelo signal (Figure 4E and F) as well as a C/G strand ratio close to what was seen in U2OS cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by ssTelo FISH and S1-END-seq data from TRF1-FokI expressing cells.

claim: Accumulation of single-stranded telomeric DNA is tightly linked to the ALT process itself.
source: Collectively, these data show that cells undergoing ALT have multiple single-stranded DNA regions that vastly exceed the number of chromosome ends. Accumulation of single-stranded telomeric DNA is tightly linked to the ALT process itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of ALT-positive, BLM-deficient, and TRF1-FokI expressing cells.

claim: END-seq can efficiently capture 5′ chromosome termini.
source: Here, we show that END-seq can efficiently capture 5′ chromosome termini, providing a high-resolution and unbiased approach to studying the terminal portion of chromosome ends.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation of END-seq throughout the manuscript.

claim: END-seq does not rely on capture oligos and can be applied to telomeres of any length.
source: END-seq has several advantages over alternative approaches: it is unbiased since it does not rely on capture oligos, it can be applied to telomeres of any length, and does not require any prior knowledge of the subtelomeric sequence.
evidence: This describes the technical advantages of the END-seq method.

claim: The ATC-5′ sequence appears to be universal across mammalian cells.
source: These data show that the ATC-5′ sequence appears to be universal, highlighting a conserved mechanism of end-processing in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is inferred from END-seq data across multiple mammalian species.

claim: ALT-positive cells use recombination-based mechanisms for telomere elongation.
source: Our data show that ALT-positive cells, which use recombination-based mechanisms for telomere elongation, have the same regulation of terminal repeats as telomerase-positive cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ALT mechanism.

claim: The regulation of the terminal 5′ end of chromosome ends occurs independently of the telomere elongation mechanism.
source: This indicates that the regulation of the terminal 5′ end of chromosome ends occurs independently of the telomere elongation mechanism and that ALT-based recombination does not alter this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of terminal sequences in ALT and non-ALT cells.

claim: POT1 is critical in U2OS cells to define the 5′ end termini of telomeres.
source: Furthermore, our data show that POT1 is critical, even in U2OS cells, to define the 5′ end termini of telomeres.
evidence: This is supported by POT1 depletion experiments in U2OS cells.

claim: The presence of single-stranded telomeric DNA characterizes ALT-positive cells.
source: Using the unbiased S1-END-seq approach, we show that the presence of single-stranded telomeric DNA characterizes ALT-positive cells.
evidence: This is supported by S1-END-seq data from multiple ALT-positive cell lines.

claim: Cells can be readily classified as ALT-positive or ALT-negative based on the occurrence of S1-cuts within the telomeric reads.
source: This property of ALT is unique in that cells can be readily classified as ALT-positive or ALT-negative based on the occurrence of S1-cuts within the telomeric reads (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the distinct S1-END-seq patterns observed in ALT vs non-ALT cells.

claim: The observed single-stranded telomeric DNA may arise from R-loops, D-loops, internal DNA loops (i-loops), and extrachromosomal circles.
source: The observed single-stranded telomeric DNA may arise from various sources, including R-loops, D-loops, internal DNA loops (i-loops), and extrachromosomal circles, which are known to be prevalent in ALT (Dilley et al., 2016; Henson et al., 2009; Mazzucco et al., 2020; Arora et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on known ALT features and supported by citations.

claim: Previous indirect evidence suggested that ALT-positive cells exhibit increased levels of telomeric ssDNA, RPA-staining, and FISH under native conditions.
source: Notably, our findings align with previous indirect evidence suggesting that ALT-positive cells exhibit increased levels of telomeric ssDNA, RPA-staining, and FISH under native conditions (Loe et al., 2020; Grudic et al., 2007; Claude et al., 2021; Frank et al., 2022).
evidence: This references previous work that is now confirmed by the current study.

claim: There are at least five distinct regions of single-stranded DNA for each chromosome end in ALT-positive cells.
source: However, based on the relative ratio between G-rich and C-rich strands, we estimate that there are at least five distinct regions of single-stranded DNA for each chromosome end in ALT-positive cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is estimated from the C/G strand ratio analysis.

claim: The frequency of VTRs is higher in the internal portions of chromosome ends compared to the terminal portions in U2OS cells.
source: We compared the frequency of VTRs within the first 30 nucleotides of the S1-END-seq reads from U2OS libraries (3.8%) to their control END-seq U2OS libraries (1.93%). This shows that the frequency of VTRs is higher in the internal portions of chromosome ends compared to the terminal portions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on comparison of VTR frequencies in END-seq vs S1-END-seq data.

claim: Depletion of BLM is sufficient to suppress ALT-mediated telomere elongation.
source: Depletion of BLM is sufficient to suppress ALT-mediated telomere elongation, as shown by the loss of ALT-associated features and progressive telomere shortening (Jiang et al., 2024; Loe et al., 2020; O'Sullivan et al., 2014; Min et al., 2019; Sobinoff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: BLM helicase contributes to telomere stability by resolving secondary structures and ensures proper telomeres replication regardless of telomere maintenance mechanism.
source: Given that BLM helicase contributes to telomere stability by resolving secondary structures and ensures proper telomeres replication regardless of telomere maintenance mechanism (Barefield and Karlseder, 2012; Drosopoulos et al., 2015; Sfeir et al., 2009), it is possible that ssDNA detected in the absence of BLM is due to replication fidelity.
evidence: This is speculation based on known BLM functions supported by citations.

claim: Expression of TRF1-Fok1 results in DSBs at telomeres, which are detected as the appearance of G-rich reads by END-seq in both BLM-proficient and BLM-deficient cells.
source: Expression of TRF1-Fok1 results in DSBs at telomeres, which are detected as the appearance of G-rich reads by END-seq in both BLM-proficient and BLM-deficient cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by END-seq data from TRF1-FokI expressing cells.

claim: Cells undergoing ALT have multiple single-stranded DNA regions that vastly exceed the number of chromosome ends.
source: Collectively, these data show that cells undergoing ALT have multiple single-stranded DNA regions that vastly exceed the number of chromosome ends.
evidence: This is inferred from the S1-END-seq data showing multiple ssDNA regions per chromosome end.

claim: Pan-centromeric sequences are not enriched to the same level as telomeres nor show any strand bias when detected by END-seq.
source: To exclude possible artifacts derived from the repetitive nature of telomeric reads, we performed a similar analysis of reads corresponding to pan-centromeric repeats; this analysis shows that although the fraction of their presence in the human genome was similar (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), the pan-centromeric sequences are not enriched to the same level as telomeres nor show any strand bias when detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a control experiment to validate the specificity of END-seq for telomeres.

claim: T7 exonuclease preferentially degrades 5′ ends of double-stranded DNA while leaving 3′ single-stranded overhangs intact.
source: Since T7 exonuclease preferentially degrades 5′ ends of double-stranded DNA while leaving 3′ single-stranded overhangs intact, we expected that its treatment would randomize the 5′ telomeric ends by progressively resecting them, thereby disrupting the original sequence bias.
evidence: This describes the known enzymatic activity of T7 exonuclease.

claim: In POT1-proficient and POT1b-depleted mouse ESC samples, approximately 70% and 85% of reads, respectively, corresponded to the perfect canonical ends.
source: Using the KL divergence score, we determined that in the POT1-proficient and POT1b-depleted samples, approximately 70% and 85% of reads, respectively, corresponded to the perfect canonical ends.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of END-seq data from mouse ESCs.

claim: In POT1a-depleted mouse ESC samples, approximately 25% of reads corresponded to the perfect canonical ends, regardless of POT1b status.
source: In contrast, in POT1a-depleted samples, this proportion was around 25%, regardless of POT1b status.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of END-seq data from POT1a-depleted mouse ESCs.

claim: Positive staining for the single-strand binding protein RPA and native FISH staining (ssTelo) of telomeres suggested the presence of single-stranded DNA regions in ALT-positive cells.
source: Interestingly, positive staining for the single-strand binding protein RPA and native FISH staining (ssTelo) of telomeres suggested the presence of single-stranded DNA regions in ALT-positive cells (Loe et al., 2020; Grudic et al., 2007).
evidence: This references previous indirect evidence for ssDNA in ALT cells.

claim: EM data and rolling-circle amplification-based assays suggest that ALT frequently contain circular extrachromosomal telomeric DNA termed C-circles.
source: Intriguingly, EM data and rolling-circle amplification-based assays suggest that ALT frequently contain circular extrachromosomal telomeric DNA termed C-circles (Henson et al., 2009; Cesare and Griffith, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ALT cells supported by citations.

claim: S1 nuclease is an enzyme that specifically degrades single-stranded DNA including the single-stranded regions in duplex DNA.
source: Secondly, to assess the presence of ssDNA at ALT telomeres, we used S1 nuclease, an enzyme that specifically degrades single-stranded DNA including the single-stranded regions in duplex DNA.
evidence: This describes the known enzymatic activity of S1 nuclease.

claim: The presence of ssDNA in telomeres can be used to distinguish ALT-positive from ALT-negative cells.
source: Using S1 nuclease treatment coupled with END-seq (S1-END-seq) (Matos-Rodrigues et al., 2022), we show that ALT telomeres have tracts of ssDNA and the presence of ssDNA in telomeres can be used to distinguish ALT-positive from ALT-negative cells.
evidence: This is supported by S1-END-seq data showing distinct patterns in ALT vs non-ALT cells.

claim: ALT telomeres have tracts of ssDNA.
source: Using S1 nuclease treatment coupled with END-seq (S1-END-seq) (Matos-Rodrigues et al., 2022), we show that ALT telomeres have tracts of ssDNA and the presence of ssDNA in telomeres can be used to distinguish ALT-positive from ALT-negative cells.
evidence: This is supported by S1-END-seq data from ALT cells.

claim: END-seq is an unbiased sequencing-based approach to define the identity and regulation of the terminal sequences of chromosomes.
source: To address this, we adopted END-seq, an unbiased sequencing-based approach, to define the identity and regulation of the terminal sequences of chromosomes in ALT cells.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: END-seq was originally developed to map and investigate double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: To study the terminal portion of chromosome, we employed an unbiased and high-resolution approach developed to map and investigate double-strand breaks (DSBs): END-seq (Canela et al., 2016).
evidence: This references the original purpose of the END-seq method.

claim: In END-seq, biotin-labeled adaptors are ligated to DSBs, which enable their purification and subsequent sequencing by next-generation sequencing.
source: In this method, biotin-labeled adaptors are ligated to DSBs, which enable their purification and subsequent sequencing by next-generation sequencing (NGS).
evidence: This describes the technical details of the END-seq method.

claim: DSBs are identified by END-seq as unidirectional reads that originate from the lesion site on either side of the break.
source: Based on the directionality of DNA sequencing (5′ to 3′), DSBs are identified as unidirectional reads that originate from the lesion site on either side of the break (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes how END-seq detects DSBs.

claim: Chromosome ends resemble one-ended DSBs, which by END-seq should be detected as unidirectional reads corresponding to the 5′ telomeric strand, the C-rich strand.
source: Chromosome ends resemble one-ended DSBs, which by END-seq should be detected as unidirectional reads corresponding to the 5′ telomeric strand, the C-rich strand.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how END-seq should detect telomeres based on their structure.
